articles.title: Hard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British culture
articles.summary: An evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colour. Here is Kate Moss, with pink hair splayed across a pillow, her face scrubbed of makeup, her smile sweet and wonky.
body: These photos are old. They were taken a long time ago. But they’re young, too. They are curated by Edward Enninful for the Tate’s exhibition The 90s: Art and Fashion (Enninful worked at i-D in the 90s) and almost everyone involved is shiny and fresh. The models, whether professional or not, are mostly in their 20s, and the photographers are early in their careers. It gives the photos a youthful fizz, a verve. But the energy also comes from an understanding between photographer and subject. In many of the pictures you can feel the shared mischief, a “yes we’re serious about our ideas” but also a “look, we’re getting away with it!” delight.

Parties were plentiful. Aside from the club scene, magazines threw them, art galleries threw them, some random person that you met in a late-night drinking den said, “I know this place”, so you went. When you were out, you met artists, photographers, musicians, actors, writers, promoters, dealers, “entrepreneurs”. Often you had no idea what they did: I once walked into an office and realised that the esteemed head of design was the character with whom I’d spent a full-on all-nighter at Glastonbury a month before.
points: An evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colour.

articles.title: Beyond Bradford and the Brontës – new walking trail shows West Yorkshire’s natural beauty
articles.summary: The Bradford Pennine Gateway Trail, launching this weekend, aims to ‘change perceptions of Bradford’ by taking in the moors and the area’s new national nature reserve. A grainy photograph, dated 1938, hangs in a frame on the downstairs wall of my B&B.
body: I arrived here thanks to a new trail, launching on 19 September, that runs through the also newly established Bradford Pennine Gateway national nature reserve – astonishingly, the first reserve of this kind to be created in West Yorkshire. The trail uses almost the same name and is a savvy bit of sustainable planning, connecting the three towns of Ilkley, Saltaire and Haworth but, by appealing to walkers, hopefully inspiring people to explore beyond the confines of these honeypots.

I began at Ilkley on a Monday morning. I’d been on its moor once before, for a long circular hike. But I actually prefer linear walks, and it felt like a challenge to start out by crossing the moor. The first half hour was all upward, with lots of stone staircases and some steep sections. A hovering kestrel welcomed me to the top as a reward.
points: The Bradford Pennine Gateway Trail, launching this weekend, aims to ‘change perceptions of Bradford’ by taking in the moors and the area’s new national nature reserve.

articles.title: You be the judge: should my brother have told me the money I lent him was for his holiday?
articles.summary: Ayaan thought she was lending money for something essential. Ahmed says the lender doesn’t get to dictate what it’s spent on. You decide who is on the money. • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror. I thought I was lending Ahmed money for something vital, not a trip to Greece.
body: My brother Ahmed and I both live at home – he’s 27 and I’m 25. I look up to him, but he’s much more disorganised than me, and over the years has asked me to keep secrets from our parents when he’s messed up. I lent him money recently, which he then used to go on holiday with his friends. It annoyed me, but I didn’t tell our parents.

Ahmed is between jobs right now. I am doing a journalism internship, but at least I have a wage. When Ahmed asked me for the money he didn’t say what it was for, but I assumed it was living expenses or something essential. Our parents work but send money home to family in Somalia, so we try to help out with the rent. Ahmed hasn’t been paying much recently but my parents don’t mind as they want him to find work. Also, I think that as the eldest son, he gets away with more.

Ahmed and I are close but we don’t talk in detail about our finances. I assumed that for him to have to ask me for money, it was vital. I lent him £400 a month or so ago, which is a lot out of my monthly internship pay of £1,500. We didn’t discuss terms or when he would repay me, but I thought it would be sooner rather than later.
points: Ayaan thought she was lending money for something essential.

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake | A kitchen in Rome
articles.summary: A 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursome. Yesterday’s lunch and this week’s recipe is thanks to my friend, the designer Jake Tilson, who gave me a pristine 1977 edition of The Talisman Italian Cook Book.
body: I don’t regret making the recipe from page 161 for rice with aubergine, however, which I have adapted for variety’s sake. This bake is good when made with tinned tomatoes, but fresh ones bring a brighter burst of flavour. Ideally, try to get a mix of varieties – a few sweet cherries, a couple of plums, a big fleshy one – that have been peeled and cooked into a sweet-savoury sauce; if necessary, add a pinch of sugar.

A reason for eating this pretty much straight out of the oven and while it’s still steaming hot is the mozzarella, because the cheese is molten and pulls into those long strings that make serving it and eating it so entertaining. The benefit of waiting half an hour or longer is that the flavours develop, while the bake itself (and the mozzarella inside and on top) firms up. Or serve at whatever stage or temperature you like, with whatever variety of salad or vegetable.

Using a peeler, pare strips of skin from the aubergines so they are striped, then cut into 1cm-thick slices. Arrange these on an oiled baking tray, zigzag with more oil, sprinkle with salt, then bake at 180C (160C)/350F/gas 4 for 30-40 minutes, until tender and a little golden.
points: A 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursome.

articles.title: London Fashion Week Cheat Sheet: Spring/Summer 2027
articles.summary: With plenty of new names on the schedule and an Alexander McQueen homecoming, SS27 could be a landmark London Fashion Week.
body: London Fashion Week (LFW) is fast approaching, and the schedule is tight, bolstered with a slew of activations, parties and dinners. Comparative to New York, it’s a lighter load, but the mix of big-ticket shows and emerging independents — many eschewing the runway format for experiential events — continues to position the city as a springboard for hot, young talent and heritage stalwarts.

“We are opening up London Fashion Week to new energy, new ideas and new ways of engaging with fashion,” says Laura Weir, the British Fashion Council's CEO. “Alongside traditional catwalk formats, the schedule features everything from [Californian brand] 5000’s multisensory sound bath to AllSaints ’s zine launch. That breadth is deliberate. London Fashion Week is a global platform for designers and businesses, but it is also a way of demonstrating the wider cultural and economic value of fashion. By bringing together fashion, art, music, technology, retail, and culture, we are demonstrating the sector’s reach, relevance and ability to create value far beyond the catwalk.”
points: With plenty of new names on the schedule and an Alexander McQueen homecoming, SS27 could be a landmark London Fashion Week.

articles.title: The Fashion Exec’s Guide to New York Climate Week
articles.summary: New York Climate Week is just around the corner. Here are the defining themes and events you can’t miss.
body: Once a year, New York Climate Week comes to town, bringing a melting pot of industries, celebrities, activists and policymakers with it. Hot on the heels of New York Fashion Week, with some events bleeding into the week itself, this year’s climate week is seemingly more jam-packed than ever.

With over 1,000 events on the official schedule, and many more unofficial gatherings alongside, Vogue Business called on insiders to help you make sense of it all. Here are the key themes fashion will be grappling with throughout the week and the can’t-miss events on their radars.

There are several closed-door sessions on the agenda this year, as climate week joins the growing line-up of other sustainable fashion conferences leaning into off-record roundtables to drive candor and progress. “This year, I’m doing invite-only, curated rooms instead of running myself ragged across every panel,” says Rachel Kibbe, CEO of American Circular Textiles (AMCIRC). “My advice to other execs would be to pick your rooms and don’t try to do it all.”
points: New York Climate Week is just around the corner.

articles.title: 9 Pet-Friendly Hotels in Savannah Where Your Dog Gets the Five-Star Treatment
articles.summary: From dog-friendly patios to dedicated pup menus, these Savannah hotels make it easy to bring your four-legged friend along for the ride.
body: I love my dog, but she’s not exactly a great traveler. If she were, one of the first places I'd bring her would be Savannah —a city I visit often from my base in Atlanta —where she could sniff her way through one of the nation’s most beautiful historic cities. Whenever I’m in the Hostess City, I can’t help but notice how welcoming it is to dogs, with pups dotting the lush squares and lounging on restaurant patios at places like the Collins Quarter in Forsyth Park and Foxy Loxy Cafe in the Starland District. Even famed Leopold’s Ice Cream makes special sundaes for furry friends to enjoy alfresco.

It’s no surprise, then, that plenty of hotels in town welcome four-legged guests, too. And bringing your dog doesn’t mean sacrificing luxury or hospitality at the best pet-friendly hotels in Savannah. The properties below pair stylish accommodations and thoughtful service with amenities for pups, easy access to green space, and, in some cases, even special menus. Here are nine pet-friendly hotels in Savannah, GA where your dog can feel right at home.

articles.title: Inside TIFF’s 2026 Road to the Golden Globes Party
articles.summary: Andrew Scott, Léa Seydoux, Colman Domingo, Naomi Watts, Sarah Paulson, Gemma Chan, and more gathered at the Four Seasons Hotel Toronto for TIFF’s star-studded Road to the Golden Globes party.
body: Among the night’s more unexpected guests was former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, who came bearing a new title: producer. Days earlier, he had unveiled his new media company with a slate of scripted series and documentaries already in development. Trudeau was spotted chatting with Watts and Paulson, who joined the party not long after the premiere of their estranged-sisters drama Closing Night, directed by American Horror Story actor Cody Fern and also starring Dianne Wiest.

Also circulating in the crowd were Anna Kendrick, Chloe Bailey, Seth Rogen, Courteney Cox, and Chase Infiniti, each in Toronto with a new project debuting at the festival. Elsewhere in the room, Virginie Efira, Will Sharpe, Laura Linney, Patricia Arquette, and Billie Piper were likewise in town with films on this year’s TIFF slate.

Several of the year’s most buzzed-about ensembles turned out in force. Director Lee Chang-dong was joined by his Possible Love stars, Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, and Cho Yeo-jeong, while Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi made the rounds with members of their La Bola Negra ensemble, including Spanish singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau.

articles.title: 9 Standout Galapagos Cruises for Sailing the Bucket-List Wildlife Destination
articles.summary: From luxury ships to affordable sailings, family-friendly and solo-traveler-favorites, there’s a cruise in the Galapagos for every type of traveler.
body: An extraordinary archipelago 600 miles off the coast of Ecuador, the Galapagos promise a once-in-a-lifetime travel experience—and many agree there's no better way to visit, than by ship. Unlike the typical island-hopping cruise itinerary you'll find elsewhere, Galapagos Island cruises invite travelers to experience some of the most unspoiled environments on earth. The vessels here are small, too—sometimes accommodating as few as 16 passengers. There are no water parks, Broadway-style shows, or casinos on board. Instead, pristine surroundings, uninhabited islands, and rare wildlife are the featured attractions.

articles.title: Can an Arnault Help Revive Nike?
articles.summary: Alexandre Arnault, an LVMH heir with experience at Moët, Tiffany and Rimowa, has been appointed to Nike’s board as the brand struggles to find its footing on a path forward.
body: Nike has a new board member in Alexandre Arnault, the second son of Bernard Arnault and who is currently the deputy CEO of Moët Hennessy, LVMH’s wines and spirits division.

“Alexandre has earned a reputation for helping iconic global brands evolve, innovate and grow in a changing, complex marketplace,” said Nike executive chair Mark Parker on Wednesday. “As part of our commitment to strong governance and thoughtful board succession, we look for leaders with distinctive experiences, fresh perspectives and a proven ability to create long-term value. Alexandre’s leadership across some of the world’s most respected brands will make him a strong addition to our board.”
Nike’s board of directors has its fair share of blockbuster names — like co-founder Phil Knight, and Apple chair and former CEO Tim Cook — but, until now, none that come from the luxury space.

articles.title: Hoy Is Bringing Night-Market Energy to NYC
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. This is the first installment of our series Getting on the Map, presented by Apple Maps.
body: When I spoke with Cyed Adraincem, he apologized for stumbling over any words; he’d been up at 4 a.m. to wash the sidewalk in front of his forthcoming restaurant. “I wanted to beat all the foot traffic,” he said.

Adraincem seems to have brought that same dedication to outfitting Hoy, which will serve Filipino street food in a Manila night-market-like space. Though not yet open, the restaurant has already garnered a lot of attention for its loud and off-kilter aesthetic, smart pop cultural ties, and behind-the-scenes peeks into R&D. I asked him about designing the space, the merch plan, and how opening is going.

Cyed Adraincem: It’s Filipino street food, super fast casual. I’m trying to introduce Filipino food to a broader audience because I feel like we’re underrepresented in New York City. We’ll be serving barbecue skewers, lumpia, and a couple different sandwiches. It’s a pretty simple menu, nothing too fancy, mostly traditional, with chef techniques that we’ve learned over the years. I think the New York dining scene wants something more casual, more affordable right now. They don’t want something pretentious; they just want to eat and have a good drink.
